walkthroughs.body_html:
Themes in Economics — a core area of A-Level Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Themes in Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Themes in Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Are monopolies always bad for consumers?
options: Standard theory says monopolies restrict output and raise prices, but possible benefits include economies of scale, R&D investment and dynamic efficiency.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.
Monopolies are illegal and always harmful.

mcqs.q: What does Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) tell us?
options: The sign tells us the good type: positive YED = normal good (rises with income); negative YED = inferior good (falls with income). YED > 1 indicates a luxury; YED between 0 and 1 a necessity.
YED measures how the rich and poor differ in tastes.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A negative YED means the demand calculation went wrong.

mcqs.q: Why do economists generally argue against protectionism?
options: Protectionism always makes a country richer by keeping money at home.

Tariffs and quotas raise prices for consumers, protect inefficient industries, invite retaliation, and reduce overall welfare — even when they save specific jobs, the cost per job saved typically exceeds the wage.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.
